summary:
The "gazebo" at The Spring Resort & Spa (Desert Hot Springs) is an enclosed pool pavilion. Oyster calls it "the pool inside the greenhouse". I pieced it together mainly from the resort's own photos and the ResortPass gallery, because Yelp, TripAdvisor and Hotels.com blocked automated reading. It is a single-story timber post-and-beam glass room with a low-slope roof, and it sits at one end of the main pool. The walls have three bands: a knee wall about 3 ft high, clear glass with a frosted privacy stripe, and an open band of gray-painted vertical slats under the header. A dark-bronze sliding glass door faces the main pool. Inside is a freeform pool about 4 ft deep, kept at 101F, with a blue mosaic tile band at the waterline and a pebble-finish deck. The room is furnished with wooden sling chairs, boulders, stump planters, potted yucca, a ceiling fan and a copper bowl, and it hosts weekend sound baths. A "CAPACITY 11" sign suggests about 110-120 sq ft of water if it is rated as a spa under CBC 3120B; that is my estimate. Next to it, Room 1 has its own courtyard: a tapered cast-concrete soaking tub with a brass spout, inside stained-timber screens with blue-gray panels and the same slat band. Room 9 adds a gas fire bowl and a framed glass windscreen. The resort's pergola has rough-sawn stained posts, a gray-painted lath roof, climbing vines and hanging rusted-metal cone planters. Planting is California and Mediterranean fan palms, vines trained on wires, black pebble mulch and boulders.
I also gathered six other precedents:
- **Wi Spa (LA):** five Korean hot rooms meant to be used in order, Bulgama (oak, 231F), salt, clay, jade and ice. Primary source.
- **Olympus Spa (WA):** women-only, far-infrared rooms and Himalayan salt, day passes $53-58.
- **Spa Land Centum City (Busan):** only its hours are verified.
- **Ten Thousand Waves (Santa Fe high desert):** private suites with a tub, sauna and cold plunge, including a "Shoji" tub of 6x6 ft at 104F and a 9x4 ft slate ofuro, $89 per person for 90 minutes.
- **Two Bunch Palms:** a seclusion-and-grotto ethos.
- **Korakia:** Moroccan courtyards and a copper cold-plunge tub.
- **Hanok, jeongja and hanji:** open-sided garden pavilions, long eaves that manage sun, and hanji-papered doors.
The design ideas combine The Spring's glass, slat and timber room with the Korean hot-to-cold order and an ondol-style heated platform. Shoji-style screens in coral, backed by waterproof polycarbonate about 2 mm thick, would glow blush at night. Caveats: the dimensions are estimates from photos. My web-search budget ran out partway through, so the Spa Land details and the changsal pattern names are not confirmed from primary sources. This topic also sits outside the RV-trailer request that was passed to me. The only link is the phase-0 idea of a soak next to the trailer.

findings.title: The Spring's enclosed pool: official temperatures and the 'greenhouse' description
findings.detail: The resort's own day-spa page says: 'The enclosed soaking pool is maintained slightly above body temperature. An outdoor soaking pool is maintained at 104 degrees. The large, sparkling swimming pool's temperature is adjusted to weather conditions.' Hot-spring guides give 101F indoors, 104F for the outdoor jacuzzi and 88-90F for the big pool. Source water rises at 170F and is cooled. Oyster says: 'The pool inside the greenhouse is just above body temperature.' The property was built in 1957 as The Moors Hotel and renamed The Spring in 2003. It is adults-only (18+), and overnight guests get 24-hour access to the pools and sauna.

findings.title: Gazebo form reconstructed from photos: timber post-and-beam glass pavilion
findings.detail: From the gallery photo of the main pool (Spring-Spa-Full-Size-12-1) and ResortPass photo 3207, seen from outside. It is a rectangular one-story pavilion at the end of the main pool, next to a 'Pool Rules: CAPACITY 40' sign. The roof is low-slope with a thin metal fascia and exposed gray-painted rafter tails. Posts and header are stained timber (orange-brown, probably cedar or Douglas fir). The wall facing the pool is a fixed glass pane plus a dark-bronze aluminum sliding glass door. Under the header runs a band about 1 ft tall of gray or white painted vertical slats with dark gaps. From the Room 1 side (Spring-Spa-Full-Size-13), the same pavilion shows glass panels with a frosted horizontal privacy stripe, roller cassettes above the glass (I cannot tell whether they hold solar screen or clear vinyl), and a slatted clerestory under a deeper timber header. Fan palms stand right beside it. Estimated from photos, not measured: posts about 5.5-6 ft apart, knee wall about 3 ft, glass about 3.5 ft, slat band about 1 ft, top plate about 7.5-8 ft.

findings.title: Gazebo interior: freeform 4-ft pool, pebble deck, sling chairs, sound baths
findings.detail: ResortPass photo 3206, captioned 'Indoor heated pool with lane dividers, wooden chairs, and palm plants visible', and the resort's gallery4 ('sound bath') show the interior. The pool is freeform and lobed, with '4' depth markers, a dark-blue glass mosaic band at the waterline, a wide light-colored bullnose concrete coping, dark-blue tile lines on the pool floor, and entry steps. The deck is light exposed aggregate (pebble finish). Six or so wooden folding sling chairs line the walls, along with boulders, a cut-log stump planter, woven baskets, potted yucca or dracaena and sansevieria, and a copper or bronze bowl (fountain or fire bowl) on the coping. There is a ceiling fan, a wall clock, small sconces, and signs reading 'CAPACITY 11' and '911'. Inside, the walls are stained posts with blue-gray painted battens framing pale, softly lit panels that may be translucent; this is inferred. Crystal and Tibetan singing bowls are set out on the deck for weekend sound baths. The resort site lists the Saturday sound bath at $65, Sunday yoga at $25, and a $150 package that includes 2 hours of soaking.

findings.title: Size inferred from the posted capacity sign and California code
findings.detail: CBC Title 24 Part 2 §3120B.2.1 sets spa-pool capacity at one user per 10 sq ft of water surface. §3120B.2.2 sets other pools at one per 20 sq ft. The enclosed pool's 'CAPACITY 11' sign therefore implies about 110-119 sq ft of water if it is rated as a spa, which fits its 101F temperature and 4 ft depth. If it is rated as a regular pool, it would be about 220-239 sq ft. The main pool's 'CAPACITY 40' implies about 800 sq ft. Low-resolution Esri imagery at the resort's Google pin (33.95569, -116.48258) shows a courtyard pool of roughly 5.5 x 12 m, which is consistent. These are inferences, not measured dimensions.

findings.title: Courtyard tubs at Room 1 and Room 9: concrete soaking tubs, screens, fire bowl, windscreen
findings.detail: The rooms page says: 'The Courtyard Suite has a private patio with a mineral water soaking tub.' It also says Room 9 'has an exclusive mineral water soaking tub in its patio area as well as a personal fire pit.' Room 1's photo (room-1.jpg, the same shot as Full-Size-13) shows a tapered cast-concrete tub with a trowel texture, about 6 x 3.5 ft by estimate. A brass spigot pours mineral water into it, and a two-step wood stool stands alongside. The screen walls are stained-timber frames with blue-gray textured infill panels and the same slat top band. The ground is black pebble mulch with a boulder, Mediterranean fan palms and a small tree. The Room 9 night photo shows a concrete tub, a copper gas fire bowl, and a stacked-stone seat wall with a wood bench top. Behind them are a stucco wall with vines trained on vertical wires, large concrete pavers set in black river pebbles, and a timber-framed glass windscreen with a slat top facing the mountains. Candles provide the light.

findings.title: Pergola, palms and garden vocabulary at The Spring
findings.detail: The ResortPass caption reads 'Outdoor pergola lounge with wooden beams, black loungers, and climbing ivy plants'. The photo shows rough-sawn stained posts and beam, a gray-painted lath roof, dense vines on the building wall, hanging rusted-metal cone planters, and cut-log side tables. The resort describes 'the tranquil courtyard, rich with aromas of fragrant blossoms. Palms and desert foliage grace the three sparkling mineral pools', 'the shade of the old palm trees', and 'the outdoor fire pit'. Gallery photos show tall California fan palms, Mediterranean fan palms, ornamental grasses, boulders, decomposed granite and gravel, and Adirondack chairs around the 104F spa, which has a stainless handrail. There is also a 'Shhh... Quiet Please' sign in wood. The resort keeps a quiet, no-TV, no-phone-call culture.

findings.title: I could not confirm the quoted 'pool inside the gazebo' review
findings.detail: Yelp and TripAdvisor returned 403 errors and Hotels.com returned 503s, so I could not read their reviews. One search snippet mentioned a TripAdvisor review saying 'my favorite was the pool in the gazebo', but it did not name the resort. A Hotels.com snippet described 'a spacious bathtub surrounded by a glass-walled enclosure and a wooden pergola', which matches Room 1's tub court. The reconstruction above relies on photos and official text rather than review wording.

findings.title: Wi Spa (Los Angeles): five Korean hot rooms used in order
findings.detail: Wi Spa is open 24/7 at 2700 Wilshire Blvd. It has separate men's and women's floors, a co-ed family jjimjilbang and a rooftop terrace. Its site says to visit five rooms 'in progression'. BULGAMA is 'made mostly out of oak wood, sits at an impressive 231 degrees', with 10-15 minutes recommended. SALT is halotherapy with minerals. CLAY uses 'clay specially imported from Korea… Guests immerse their bodies under layers of clay balls'. JADE is 'powerfully hot', with 'sodium and minerals within the walls'. The ICE room is 'the final stop'. The jjimjilbang is described as 'the common, co-ed area that is the traditional center of Korean spas'.

findings.title: Korean jjimjilbang typology
findings.detail: Wikipedia: bathing areas are separated by gender, with 'hot tubs, showers, Korean traditional kiln saunas'. Kiln rooms are themed jade, salt or mineral and run '15 to 50 °C (60 to 120 °F)', with the temperature posted at each entrance. Unisex floors have 'ondol-heated floors for lounging and sleeping'. Guests wear T-shirt-and-shorts uniforms color-coded by gender. Korean Wikipedia describes the traditional kiln as a stone dome heated with pine firewood at about 50-90°C, and says the modern combined bath-and-jjimjil format appeared in Busan around 1993. That section has no citations.

findings.title: Olympus Spa (Lynnwood and Tacoma, WA): women-only Korean spa
findings.detail: The site is titled 'Exclusive Spa for Women'. Facilities include hydrotherapy pools, a steam room, and far-infrared heated relaxation rooms using 'health-promoting materials such as Himalayan salt'. Lynnwood has 'eight unique relaxation rooms' and Tacoma has four. Day passes are $58 at Lynnwood and $53 at Tacoma. Reviewers mention pools at roughly 90F and 104F, heated floors in the tea and reading rooms, and a cool 'cabin room'.

findings.title: Spa Land Centum City (Busan): only partly verified
findings.detail: The official Shinsegae Centum City page lists 'ㆍ스파랜드(1F) : 09:00~22:00(입장마감 21:00)', meaning Spa Land on the 1st floor is open 9am-10pm with last entry at 9pm, and spa visitors get 4 hours of free parking. Wikivoyage lists a 4-hour limit and ₩12,000 weekday / ₩14,000 weekend entry; those prices are probably out of date. My web-search budget ran out, so I could not confirm from a primary source the commonly cited details: hot-spring water drawn from about 1,000 m deep, about 13 themed jjimjilbang rooms, and an outdoor foot spa. Treat those as unverified.

findings.title: Ten Thousand Waves (Santa Fe high desert): Japanese private bath suites
findings.detail: The spa was founded in 1981 as 'a small bathhouse, eight outdoor hippie hot tubs'. Each private suite is described as a 'totally self-contained bathing environment with a hot tub, sauna, and your own private changing room and shower'. Shoji ('Modern Japanese design reinterpreted for the high desert'): 'Six foot by six foot tile and stainless steel bath (104 degrees F.)', maximum 4 people, an architectural-concrete radiant wet/dry sauna at 175-185F, and a 'Walk-in private cold plunge (45-55 degrees F.)' that 'glows blue'. Ofuro: 'Nine foot by four foot slate Japanese soaking tub', where 'A roof protects you; but there are views across the valley from the open balcony'. Ichiban: 'two hand-thrown ceramic tubs' in a garden at 104F. Waterfall: a free-form polished concrete and rock bath for up to 10. Private suites cost $89 per person for 90 minutes; reserved community soaking is $64.

findings.title: Two Bunch Palms and Korakia: desert seclusion precedents
findings.detail: Two Bunch Palms (Desert Hot Springs) says its springs come 'from a 600-year-old aquifer' and 'emerge naturally at over 100 degrees, fully replenishing themselves every 24 hours'. It describes guests 'retreating into the grotto's steaming waters or the shade of its iconic palms', with a brand built on seclusion. The Al Capone hideout story is presented as legend. Korakia (Palm Springs) began in the 1920s when painter Gordon Coutts 'built a Moroccan hideaway'. It has 'secret gardens, pools, lounges, and fountains among 28 villas', two saltwater pools, 'high wood beam ceilings', a stone bathtub, and a sauna cold plunge in 'a striking copper tub'.

findings.title: Hanok pavilions (jeongja), eaves and hanji-papered openings
findings.detail: Korean Wikipedia: jeongja were for rest, banquets and lectures, and were 'built open, without rooms or doors' so the scenery could be seen. They were sited by water or on high ground and are classed by roof form: square, hexagonal, octagonal and so on. Hanok eaves (cheoma) were 'extended long to manage sunlight and rain', and ondol together with the wooden daecheong hall regulated winter cold and summer heat. Hanji, made from paper-mulberry bark, covered door frames 'to help control room temperature'; changhoji is the paper 'used to cover doors', and 'Oiled hanji was used to make greenhouses c. 1450'. Garden examples: Soswaewon (1520s-30s), with the Jewoldang and Gwangpunggak pavilions above a stream that falls into a pond, and Hyangwonjeong (1867-73), a two-story hexagonal pavilion on an island.

findings.title: Lattice screens: modern materials for outdoor and wet use
findings.detail: Wikipedia's shoji article: modern panels use 'approximately 2 mm-thick acrylic or polycarbonate', frosted or bonded to printed film. 'Plastic panels are waterproof, and some may be used outdoors year-round'. Paper 'cannot be used in places where it will get wet, like a bathroom'. Modern shoji 'often… sit inside a sliding glass door or window'. Changsal pattern names (ttisal, yongjasal, ajasal 亞, wanjasal 卍, bitsal, kkotsal) are general knowledge. Every Korean-language page I tried for them returned 404, and the search budget had run out.

findings.title: California rule for a new spa at a single-family home
findings.detail: Health & Safety Code §115922 requires 'at least two of the following seven drowning prevention safety features' for a new pool or spa at a private single-family home. One listed feature is a safety cover labeled to ASTM F1346-23. Per the summary, pairing a safety cover with a pool alarm does not satisfy the two-feature rule; verify that with the County.

design_numbers: The Spring water temperatures: enclosed pool 101F ('slightly above body temperature'), outdoor spa 104F, main pool 88-90F (adjusted for weather), spring source 170F (the-spring.com/spa/day-spa; hotspringsguides.com)

The Spring's enclosed pool has '4' ft depth markers and a 'CAPACITY 11' sign. At the CBC §3120B.2.1 spa rate of 1 user per 10 sq ft, that means about 110-119 sq ft of water (my estimate); at the regular-pool rate of 1 per 20 sq ft, about 220-239 sq ft
The Spring main pool has a 'CAPACITY 40' sign, which works out to about 800 sq ft of water at 1 per 20 sq ft. Esri imagery suggests roughly 5.5 x 12 m (estimate)

Pavilion wall layout estimated from photos, not measured: posts about 5.5-6 ft apart; knee wall about 36 in; clear glass about 42 in with a frosted privacy stripe near eye level; slat band about 10-12 in; top plate about 7.5-8 ft; low-slope roof with exposed rafter tails

Room 1 concrete tub: tapered sides, about 6 ft x 3.5 ft by photo estimate. At an assumed 3.5 ft water depth, a 6x6 ft tub holds about 126 cu ft, or roughly 940 gal (my calculation); a 6x3.5 ft tub holds about 550 gal
Ten Thousand Waves Shoji tub: 6 ft x 6 ft, tile and stainless, 104F, max 4 people (can be cooled to 99F); sauna 175-185F; cold plunge 45-55F
Ten Thousand Waves Ofuro tub: 9 ft x 4 ft slate, neck-deep, max 4 people; roof plus open balcony
Wi Spa Bulgama hot room: oak, 231F, 10-15 min. Salt, clay, jade and ice rooms: 10-20 min each, used in order
Jjimjilbang kiln rooms 60-120F (15-50C) per English Wikipedia; traditional pine-fired stone kiln 50-90C per Korean Wikipedia
The Spring infrared sauna 120-150F with six-color chromotherapy lights; its Finnish sauna rocks are fire-heated
Shoji-style screen infill: about 2 mm acrylic or polycarbonate, frosted or film-backed; plastic panels are waterproof and some can be used outdoors year-round
CA Health & Safety Code §115922: a new spa at a single-family home needs at least 2 of 7 drowning-prevention features; a safety cover counts if labeled to ASTM F1346-23

Proposed pavilion for the Yucca Valley lot (my proposal, not sourced): 3 x 3 bays at about 5 ft 4 in, giving 16 x 16 ft (256 sq ft), or a compact 12 x 16 ft; eaves projecting 30-36 in to shade the high summer sun; slat clerestory left open for steam venting
The Spring's main pool is fully booked at times, so the resort caps attendance; overnight guests get 24-hour access, day spa runs 9am-7pm

risks.risk: The gazebo dimensions and materials come from photos and a capacity sign, not measurements. The photos date from 2019, and the pavilion may have changed since.
risks.mitigation: Buy an $84 half-day pass. Pace and photograph the pavilion and Room 1's court, and ask staff who built it and what the wall panels are.

risks.risk: Wanjasal (卍) lattice can read as a swastika to US visitors and could undermine the brand.
risks.mitigation: Use ajasal (亞) key-fret, ttisal, or a custom fret for the coral lattice. Leave 卍-based patterns out of signage and screens.

risks.risk: A spa or bath pavilion built before the main house may not be allowed under the County's temporary-occupancy permit, because accessory structures usually need a primary dwelling.
risks.mitigation: Confirm with San Bernardino County Land Use Services before ordering anything. Plan the pavilion as a phase after the house is finaled. During the trailer phase, keep to portable or removable pieces.

risks.risk: Drowning risk and compliance for a new spa: H&S Code §115922 requires 2 of 7 safety features.
risks.mitigation: Use an ASTM F1346-23 labeled lockable cover plus a second feature, such as an enclosure or self-closing, self-latching gate. Confirm the combination with the inspector.

risks.risk: At 3,300 ft, freezing winter nights can crack tubs and plumbing, and 100F+ summers plus dust and strong spring winds hit glass, lattice and finishes.
risks.mitigation: Use tempered glass in framed bays (like The Spring's Room 9 windscreen), polycarbonate rather than paper infill, freeze-protection circulation or drain-down, gaskets and filters against dust, and engineered post anchorage for wind.

risks.risk: Filling about 550-940 gal tubs strains a hauled-water or well budget on raw land.
risks.mitigation: Pick a 2-person tub of about 300-500 gal (estimate) and use a cover and filtration so the water is changed less often. Size against the water-supply plan.

risks.risk: Verification gaps: the web-search budget ran out, Yelp, TripAdvisor and Hotels.com were blocked, Spa Land specs are unverified, and the changsal pattern names lack a primary source.
risks.mitigation: Run more searches in a follow-up if needed, or check Spa Land and Encyclopedia of Korean Culture pages directly.

risks.risk: Scope: this spa topic sits outside the RV-trailer sourcing and budget request that was passed to this step.
risks.mitigation: Keep spa content secondary in the deliverable. The only link to the trailer is the phase-0 idea of a portable soak with a lattice windscreen next to the trailer.

next_actions: Visit The Spring (12699 Reposo Way, Desert Hot Springs). Book the $84 half-day pass, measure the enclosed pool pavilion's bays, glass, slat band and roof, and photograph Room 1's tub court and the Room 9 windscreen
Ask The Spring staff what the pavilion's wall panels and roller cassettes are (translucent panels? clear vinyl or solar screen?) and who built it
Check with San Bernardino County whether a bath pavilion, sauna or spa is allowed before the main dwelling is finaled under a temporary-occupancy permit

Choose a lattice motif (recommend ajasal 亞 key-fret or ttisal, not wanjasal 卍) and mock up a 2 ft x 4 ft coral-painted cedar panel backed with 2 mm frosted polycarbonate and blush film; test how it glows at night
Decide the tub type (cast-concrete trapezoid like The Spring vs. a 6x6 tile tub like Ten Thousand Waves vs. a packaged spa) and size it against the water budget

If wanted, spend a follow-up turn with more search budget confirming Spa Land specs and changsal pattern references from Korean primary sources (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Korea Heritage Service)
Model the four pavilion schemes in Blender using the design numbers above (task #4 in this session's list)
design_ideas: Coral changsal bath pavilion, a direct reworking of The Spring's enclosed pool room: a 16x16 ft (or 12x16 ft) black-stained timber frame on about 5 ft 4 in bays. Walls in three bands: (1) a 36 in knee wall in peach clay plaster, a hwangto nod, color #fec6b4; (2) sliding tempered-glass panels outside with sliding coral #ec4639 ajasal lattice screens inside, backed with 2 mm frosted polycarbonate; (3) an open clerestory of black vertical slats under the header to vent steam. Low hip roof with 30-36 in eaves (cheoma) to shade the summer sun

Night glow: warm 2700K dimmable LED strips run between the polycarbonate and the lattice, so at dusk the pavilion reads as a blush-pink #f2d1d1 lantern ruled in coral lines. Add a copper gas fire bowl like The Spring's Room 9, candle niches in the knee wall, and keep all fixtures shielded and pointing down for star viewing

Korean hot-to-cold sequence on a small footprint, borrowed from Wi Spa and Ten Thousand Waves: outdoor rinse shower, then a 101-104F concrete or tile soaking tub, then a cold plunge (stock tank or tiled box), then a hot room (black cube or barrel sauna), then rest on a maru

Ondol-inspired maru: a raised 6x8 ft wood platform along the pavilion's west wall, with hydronic or electric radiant heat under it. In winter it is the jjimjilbang lounge for floor-sitting with bolsters, tea and a low table; in summer it reads as an open jeongja deck when the glass slides away

Tub court modeled on Room 1 and Room 9: a tapered cast-concrete tub with an aged-brass spout, set among 24 in concrete pavers in black Mexican beach pebbles, with one big boulder and a stacked-stone seat wall with a wood bench top. A stucco wall carries vines on vertical stainless wires

Wind and dust strategy: make the west and northwest sides solid or translucent to shelter from spring winds (prevailing direction is my assumption; verify on site). Frame the east and north in glass for morning sun, mountain views and stars, like The Spring's framed glass windscreen with a slat top

Planting that echoes The Spring but suits 3,300 ft: Mediterranean fan palm (Chamaerops humilis) by the pavilion corners, a desert willow or pomegranate as the 'garden tree', ornamental grasses, boulders and black pebble mulch. Check cold hardiness locally before buying

Pergola walkway from the house or trailer to the pavilion: rough-sawn black-stained posts with a lath roof painted blush or white, vines, and hanging rusted-steel cone planters like The Spring's pergola. Pavers lead to the bath, with bands of coral key-fret inlaid in concrete

Brand signage and objects: a small wood sign reading '쉿 · Quiet please' in a serif face with coral lettering (after The Spring's 'Shhh… Quiet Please'), white crystal singing bowls on the coping for sound baths, white towels in woven baskets, black loungers, and a coral bathing robe. These make strong high-key black-and-white photographs against the desert

Phase 0 during the trailer period: a portable soaking tub or stock-tank soak on pavers beside the trailer, sheltered by two freestanding coral ajasal windscreen panels (polycarbonate-backed, framed in black). Later the panels move into the permanent pavilion, so the trailer-period setup doubles as a full-size mockup. Confirm with the County that this is allowed under the temporary-occupancy permit
